content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.85. I used 51 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on three tasks: L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3. Then I tested four tasks:

| Test task | Rules not seen in training | Tests | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M1 (one of the trained tasks) | 0 | 10 | **12.7** (5 of the 10 were 1) |
| L1-S2-M3 (trained rules, new combination) | 0 | 16 | **26.9** |
| L4-S4-M3 | 2 | 11 | **27.6** |
| L4-S4-M4 | 3 | 11 | **27.3** |

I chose L1-S2-M3 and L4-S4-M3 because their outputs overlap with the training set by almost the same amount (0.0625 / 0.25 / 0.375 against 0.0625 / 0.1875 / 0.375). So similarity shouldn't explain any difference between them, only the number of new rules.

**Why holistic:**
- **Against part-based:** L1-S2-M3 is built only from trained rules, so a part-based learner should find it about as cheap as the trained task and clearly cheaper than the new-rule tasks. It wasn't: it cost the same as tasks with two or three new rules.
- **For holistic:** only the exact trained task got a benefit, which fits a learner that stores whole tasks.

**Limits on the conclusion:**
- The tests are very noisy: single results ranged from 1 to 57.
- Very fast results of 1 showed up on tasks with new rules too (once each for L4-S4-M3 and L4-S4-M4), so part of the noise seems to be these outliers.
- The trained task's advantage came mostly from its five results of 1. Across tasks with no trained-task advantage, cost didn't follow output overlap either. So I didn't confirm what similarity measure the holistic learner uses; the verdict rests mainly on the missing benefit for recombined tasks. That's why I put confidence at 0.85.
